Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: QA Engineer
  trauma_type: Man-made disaster
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents, Dissociative Feeling: Beginning to feel detached or unreal, Media / News: Related news
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Police: Police, Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore

Vignette:
Diego was 24, a Latin American American from a close-knit family who had built a quiet routine around his work as a QA engineer, spending most of his days testing software, tracing errors, and documenting problems before they reached users. Before the traumatic event, he had been the sort of person who liked predictable systems and clean fixes. That changed on a winter evening when he was caught in a man-made disaster that he still described with a kind of strained precision, as if getting the details exactly right might somehow make them less overwhelming. He had been in a public place when the event unfolded abruptly and violently, with people shouting, sirens converging, and the ordinary scene collapsing into confusion. In the chaos, Diego found himself thinking later that he should have done more, should have protected others and failed, even though he could not point to any single action that would have stopped what happened. What stayed with him most was not only the danger itself but the sense that, in a matter of moments, the world had become the kind of place where catastrophe could break through without warning.

In the weeks that followed, Diego noticed that certain conversations could pull him back into that night with startling force. If coworkers began talking casually about crashes, collisions, or other accidents, he felt his attention snap tight and his body go rigid, as though the room had tilted a few degrees. He would listen just long enough to become aware of the old surge of alarm, then find a reason to step away or change the subject. He also found himself avoiding police whenever possible, taking longer routes if a patrol car was parked near his building or if he saw officers on the sidewalk outside his office. What had once been ordinary public presence now felt loaded with threat; he had come to believe that you could never know who would harm you, and police cars, uniforms, and sirens no longer carried reassurance. Those encounters made him wary in a way that extended into daily life, leaving him scanning strangers more than he liked and feeling uneasy in situations that would previously have passed without comment.

The images and sensations returned most sharply through media. Diego stopped watching TV programs or films that contained accidents, disasters, or even scenes that resembled the event in any broad way, and he increasingly avoided reading about similar incidents online. At first he told himself he was just tired, but over time the pattern became more deliberate: if a headline hinted at a crash, he would close the tab; if a streaming thumbnail suggested sirens, wreckage, or panic, he would scroll past it. Even brief exposure could make him feel as if he were beginning to detach or become unreal, like the room around him was a little distant and his own body did not quite belong to him. He described this as a strange thinning of the world, an unsettling moment when he could hear his own thoughts but felt separated from them, as though he were watching himself from slightly outside.

He had also spent many hours mentally reconstructing the event in ways that always ended in the same painful conclusion. Diego would replay the sequence and imagine how life would have been different if the event had not occurred: the ordinary plans he might have kept, the ease he might have felt returning to work, the conversations that would not now be shadowed by the memory. These thoughts did not bring relief. Instead they seemed to sharpen his sense that something fundamental had been taken from him. He found it increasingly hard to imagine a future that held anything worthwhile, and at times he felt certain that nothing good could happen to him anymore. That belief showed up in small but telling ways: he turned down invitations from friends, let texts sit unanswered, and moved through his apartment with a kind of guarded resignation. As a single man, he had once been open to meeting people, but now he felt the world was too unpredictable to trust easily, and the possibility of closeness felt distant.

At work, the effects became harder to hide. QA engineering required him to focus carefully, but after hearing an accident discussed in the office kitchen or seeing a news alert about a similar event, he would lose concentration and need to reread the same lines several times. He began arranging his day to minimize exposure to anything that might remind him of the disaster, keeping his headphones in and his news notifications off. Still, reminders found him in ordinary places: a coworker’s story, a passing police car on his commute, a TV screen in the break room showing a related news segment. By the time he came to treatment, Diego was exhausted by the effort of keeping these things away and more frightened by what his own mind had come to believe—that harm could appear anywhere, that he had failed when it mattered, and that the future offered him little. What finally brought him in was the sense that his world had narrowed too far, and what he most hoped for was not to feel cured overnight, but to be able to move through his work, his neighborhood, and the rest of his life without bracing for the next reminder.
